E068-01.notes: Two independent clauses ('...in the middle of Manhattan' / 'their plan...imagined...'). A is a comma splice; C is a fused sentence; D 'Manhattan, and, their' puts an incorrect comma after the conjunction. B separates the clauses correctly with a period.

E068-02.notes: Redundancy item. B 'a lot of very many' is wordy and informal; C ('trees, many thousands of them, numerous') is redundant and awkward; D adds 'in large numbers', which repeats 'many thousands'. A is concise.

E068-03.notes: The clauses contrast: the park looks natural, but it was designed. 'Although' signals that contrast. 'Because' and 'Since' wrongly make looking natural the cause of the design. 'Unless' sets up a condition, which makes no sense here.

E068-04.notes: With B substituted, the sentence reads 'tucked roads below for crosstown traffic below the level of the park', which repeats 'below' and garbles the sentence. C 'tucked also roads' puts the adverb in an unidiomatic place. D 'also tucked, for crosstown traffic, roads below' splits the verb from its object, which is awkward. A has natural word order.

E068-05.notes: The sentence names the sunken roads and says they still carry traffic. That extends sentence 5 directly. A is wrong because nothing in the sentence concerns traffic laws. B is wrong because sentence 5 gives neither the name 'transverse roads' nor the fact that they are still in use. D is wrong because the sentence says nothing about the competition.

E068-06.notes: The phrase needs a plain plural noun as the subject of 'owned'. A 'household's' and B 'households'' are possessives with nothing to possess. C 'household' is singular and does not fit 'more than half of the Black ___ ... their land'. D 'households' is correct.

E068-07.notes: A comma should not separate the compound subject from the verb 'were', which rules out A and D. C puts a stray comma after 'and'. D also drops the serial comma inconsistently and puts a comma after 'and'. B is correct.

E068-08.notes: 'Today' and 'each year' call for the simple present tense. B 'drew' is past tense, C 'had drawn' is past perfect, and D 'will have drawn' is future perfect, so none fits the present-day frame.

E068-09.notes: Only A links the park today to Seneca Village, the cost described in paragraph 3. B lists amenities, C is about Olmsted's later career, and D gives the park's acreage; none of them connects to the human cost.

flags.note: Choice C refers to 'the transverse roads', but that term appears only in E068-05's proposed (unadded) sentence, not in the essay as printed. It is still clearly wrong because the roads are not the main focus, but the wording assumes text the essay may not contain. Consider changing it to 'the sunken crosstown roads'.

E068-10.notes: The essay covers the naturalistic design in only one paragraph, then turns to Seneca Village and eminent domain, so it would not achieve that purpose. A is wrong because the essay does not explain how each tree was chosen. C is wrong because the roads are not the main focus. D is factually wrong because sentence 4 says the park was designed.
